cards.title: String Immutability in Java
cards.content:
In Java, Strings are immutable. Once a String object is created, its value cannot be changed. Any operation that appears to modify a String actually creates a new String object in memory.

String greeting = "Hello";
greeting = greeting.concat(" World"); // Creates a new String "Hello World"

This design choice provides security, thread-safety, and allows for String pooling optimization.

cards.title: The String Constant Pool
cards.content:
To save memory, Java maintains a special execution area called the String Constant Pool inside the Heap.

  • When you declare a literal like String s = "Java";, JVM checks the pool first.
  • If it exists, the reference is reused. If not, a new object is created in the pool.
  • Using new String("Java") bypasses the pool check, forcing a new object on the heap directly.

cards.title: Essential String Methods
cards.content:
Java provides powerful built-in methods to inspect and manipulate Strings:

  • length(): Returns the number of characters.
  • charAt(int index): Retrieves char at index.
  • substring(int beginIndex, int endIndex): Extracts a segment (endIndex is exclusive).
  • indexOf(String str): Finds position of substring.
String demo = "Developer";
char ch = demo.charAt(2); // 'v'
String sub = demo.substring(0, 4); // "Deve"

cards.title: StringBuilder vs StringBuffer
cards.content:
When extensive string concatenation is needed (e.g., inside loops), String causes excessive garbage collection pressure. Java provides mutable alternatives:

  • StringBuilder: Fast, efficient, but not thread-safe. Preferred for single-threaded environments.
  • StringBuffer: Thread-safe (synchronized methods), but has performance overhead.
StringBuilder builder = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    builder.append(i);
} // "01234"

content.question: Which of the following describes the main benefit of String Immutability?

options.text: It allows String literals to be safely shared inside the String Constant Pool without synchronization issues.
It guarantees that string variables are dynamically typed at runtime.
It forces all String allocations onto Stack memory instead of Heap memory.
It allows strings to increase in size automatically without reallocation.

cards.title: String Best Practices
cards.content:
To write production-grade Java code, adhere to these key practices:

  • Null safety: When checking variables against literals, call the method on the literal: "ADMIN".equals(role) instead of role.equals("ADMIN") to prevent NullPointerException.
  • Use isEmpty() or isBlank(): Avoid manual length checks (e.g., str.length() == 0). isBlank() is especially useful as it handles whitespace characters as well.
  • Minimize internalizing: String.intern() is expensive; use it only for extremely repetitive domains.
